solution:
Count the carbons of \(\mathrm{CH_2OH-CO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\) : one in the terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\), one in the \(\mathrm{CO}\), four in \(\mathrm{(CHOH)_4}\) and one in the second terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) — seven carbons in all. The single carbonyl group is a ketonic \(\mathrm{-CO-}\) flanked by carbon on both sides, not a terminal formyl \(\mathrm{-CHO}\). Section 14.2.2 gives the naming rule : a monosaccharide with one ketonic carbonyl group is a ketose, and the name records the total number of carbons. Seven carbons plus a ketonic carbonyl gives a ketoheptose.

The other three fail on one of the two counts. Aldohexose and aldoheptose both require an aldehydic \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group, which this molecule does not have — both its ends are \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\). Ketotetrose has the right carbonyl type but only four carbons against the seven present here.

The open chain formula of glucose is \(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\) (section 14.2.4). An anomeric hydroxyl group is not present in it. Section 14.2.6 shows why : the anomeric carbon C-1 and the hydroxyl group on it come into existence only when the formyl group and the C-5 hydroxyl group close the ring to give the hemiacetal, and the two ring forms \(\alpha\)- and \(\beta\)-glucose differ precisely in the configuration of that new C-1 hydroxyl. In the open chain form C-1 is still a formyl carbon, so there is no anomeric centre and no anomeric hydroxyl.

Each of the other three is present in the open chain formula. The formyl group is the \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) at C-1. The primary hydroxyl group is the \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) at C-6 — section 14.2.4 point 6 establishes it from the oxidation of glucose and gluconic acid to the same saccharic acid. The secondary hydroxyl groups are the four \(\mathrm{-CHOH-}\) groups at C-2 to C-5.

\(\mathrm{CH_2NH_2-COOH}\) is glycine, the one \(\alpha\)-amino acid whose side chain R is simply H. Fig. 14.14 labels this structure explicitly as having an achiral \(\alpha\)-carbon : that carbon carries two hydrogen atoms, so it has two identical groups and cannot be a chiral centre. A D/L designation is assigned from the spatial arrangement about a chiral carbon, so glycine has no L-configuration at all. The description "L - amino acid" therefore does not apply, which is what the question asks for.

The other three do apply. Glycine is listed first among the neutral \(\alpha\)-amino acids in Table 14.1 — its R group carries neither a carboxyl nor an amino group, which is the chapter's test for neutral. It is entry 1 of that same table of natural \(\alpha\)-amino acids, so it is a natural amino acid. And section 14.3.1 states that an \(\alpha\)-amino acid molecule containing both an acidic \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) and a basic \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group transfers a proton from one to the other to form the dipolar zwitter ion (Fig. 14.15), which glycine does.

Section 14.3.1 defines the term directly : ten of the twenty \(\alpha\)-amino acids listed in Table 14.1 cannot be synthesised in the human body and have to be obtained through diet, and these are called essential amino acids. Tryptophan carries the asterisk in Table 14.1 that marks exactly this set. So tryptophan is called essential because the body cannot make it and it must come from food.

The other three are either true statements that are not the definition, or false. Tryptophan does contain an aromatic (indole) nucleus, but so do phenylalanine and tyrosine, and tyrosine is not marked essential — an aromatic ring is therefore not what makes an amino acid essential. "Present in all human proteins" is not something the chapter claims of tryptophan, and being widespread would not make an amino acid essential either. "Essential constituent of enzymes" reads the word essential in the wrong sense; the chapter's meaning is dietary necessity, not a role in enzyme structure.

Section 14.3.4 c lists the forces that stabilise the tertiary structure of a protein and closes with the disulfide bond : disulfide bonds formed by oxidation of nearby \(\mathrm{-SH}\) groups of cysteine residues are the covalent bonds which stabilize the tertiary structure. Fig. 14.21, the figure of tertiary structure, is labelled with a disulfide bond among its interactions. A disulfide link therefore gives rise to the tertiary structure.

The other three are stabilised by something else. The primary structure is nothing but the sequence of amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds (section 14.3.4 a) — no cross-link is involved in it. The secondary structure, the \(\alpha\)-helix and the \(\beta\)-pleated sheet, arises from hydrogen bonding between the N-H proton of one amide linkage and the C=O oxygen of another (section 14.3.4 b). The quaternary structure is the coming together of separate folded subunits, which the chapter says are held together by intermolecular forces, as in the four haeme subunits of haemoglobin.

RNA, like every nucleic acid, is a polynucleotide whose backbone consists of alternating sugar and phosphate groups joined by phosphodiester linkages (section 14.4.2 and the Remember box on printed page 319). Fig. 14.29 (b) draws that backbone in exactly the abbreviated form the option uses, \(\mathrm{-P-S-P-S-}\), with each base B hanging off a sugar. So RNA has a P-S-P-S backbone.

The other three all describe base pairing or a paired structure, and section 14.4.3 confines those to DNA : the chapter states in as many words that RNA exists as a single stranded structure, so the double-helix option is ruled out outright, and with only one strand there is nothing for a base to pair with. The A-T and C-G pairings offered by the two base-pairing options are introduced only as the complementary base pairs that hold the two strands of the DNA double helix together by hydrogen bonding. RNA does contain uracil and it does contain guanine and cytosine, but this chapter nowhere describes base pairing within RNA, so neither pairing option is supported.
